quotes.whole:
Additional Medicare tax withholding rate
Additional Medicare tax applies to an individual's Medicare wages that exceed a threshold amount based on the taxpayer's filing status. Employers are responsible for withholding the 0.9% Additional Medicare tax on an individual's wages paid in excess of $200,000 in a calendar year, without regard to filing status. An employer is required to begin withholding Additional Medicare tax in the pay period in which it pays wages in excess of $200,000 to an employee and continue to withhold it each pay period until the end of the calendar year. There's no employer match for Additional Medicare tax. For more information, see the Instructions for Form 8959 and Questions and answers for the Additional Medicare Tax.
Wage base limits
Only the Social Security tax has a wage base limit. The wage base limit is the maximum wage that's subject to the tax for that year. For earnings in 2026, this base limit is $184,500. Refer to "What's New" in Publication 15 for the current wage limit for Social Security wages.
There's no wage base limit for Medicare tax. All covered wages are subject to Medicare tax.

verdict.summary:
US Social Security contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum) for tax year 2026

ANSWER

$184,500.

For 2026, the maximum amount of earnings subject to the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax is $184,500. This is the official figure — it was announced by the Social Security Administration in the fall of 2025 as part of the 2026 automatic adjustments and has been published in final form; it is not an estimate or projection.

SCOPE / DEFINITION

- 'Contribution and benefit base' is the statutory term (Social Security Act) for the annual OASDI earnings limit. The same limit applies both to earnings subject to the OASDI tax and to earnings counted in a benefit computation — hence 'contribution and benefit base.' It is commonly called the 'taxable maximum' or 'Social Security wage base.'
- The base applies only to OASDI (Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance). Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) has had no earnings cap since 1993, so the answer to 'the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax' is the OASDI base, $184,500. Medicare tax continues on all covered wages above that amount, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages over $200,000 (employer withholding threshold).
- Self-employment (SECA): the same $184,500 base applies to the OASDI portion of net self-employment income, taxed at 12.4%.

SOURCE VERIFICATION (four independent official confirmations, all in agreement)

1. SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html): the annual table lists 2026 = $184,500 (2025 = $176,100; 2027 = $192,300).
2. SSA, Detailed Calculator update page (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html): 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500'; also gives the 'old-law' base for 2026 = $137,100 and the 2024 national average wage index = $69,846.57.
3. SSA, Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026: 'Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026 — OASDI 184,500; HI No limit.'
4. IRS Publication 15 (Circular E), Employer's Tax Guide, 2026 revision (dated Dec 15, 2025): 'The social security wage base limit is $184,500.' IRS Topic No. 751 repeats the same figure.

STATUTORY DERIVATION (confirms, rather than replaces, the published figure)

Under the automatic-adjustment formula, the base for year Y = $60,600 (the 1994 base) × (national average wage index for Y-2 ÷ NAWI for 1992), rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. For 2026, Y-2 = 2024, NAWI 2024 = $69,846.57, NAWI 1992 = $22,935.42:

  $60,600 × $69,846.57 ÷ $22,935.42 = $184,548.70 (approx.)
  $184,548.70 ÷ $300 = 615.16 → 615 × $300 = $184,500

So the formula independently reproduces $184,500. (The same page's 2027 determination, $192,300, uses NAWI 2025 = $72,800.33: $60,600 × 72,800.33 ÷ 22,935.42 = $192,353.14 → $192,300. Note that $192,300 is the 2027 figure and is not the answer to a 2026 question.)

PAYROLL CONSEQUENCES AT THE $184,500 BASE (for the 2026 tax year)

| Item | Rate | Maximum amount |
|---|---|---|
| OASDI — employee | 6.2% | $11,439.00 |
| OASDI — employer | 6.2% | $11,439.00 |
| OASDI — employee + employer (FICA) | 12.4% | $22,878.00 |
| OASDI — self-employed (SECA) | 12.4% | $22,878.00 |
| Medicare (HI) — employee and employer, each | 1.45% | No limit |
| Additional Medicare Tax — employee only | 0.9% | No limit; applies to wages over $200,000 (withholding threshold; filing-status thresholds apply on the return) |

Arithmetic check against the published data: $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439.00; × 2 = $22,878.00; × 12.4% = $22,878.00. SSA Fast Facts 2026 reports the self-employed maximum as OASI $19,557 + DI $3,321 = $22,878, which reconciles exactly with the base and rate above. No derived figure exceeds the $184,500 base.

CROSS-YEAR REFERENCE (for context only; not the answer)

1991 $53,400 … 2020 $137,700; 2021 $142,800; 2022 $147,000; 2023 $160,200; 2024 $168,600; 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500; 2027 $192,300.

OTHER 2026 THRESHOLDS THAT ARE OFTEN CONFUSED WITH THE BASE (distinct figures, not the answer)

- 'Old-law' contribution and benefit base, 2026: $137,100 (used for certain benefit computations under the pre-1977 law; not a payroll-tax cap).
- Domestic/household workers: Social Security and Medicare taxes apply if cash wages of $3,000 or more are paid in 2026.
- Election workers: $2,500 or more in cash or equivalent compensation in 2026.
- One work credit (quarter of coverage) in 2026: $1,890; four credits require $7,560.

CAVEATS

- The figure is for calendar/tax year 2026 and is fixed by statute for that year; it is not affected by an individual's filing status, age, or earnings pattern.
- Railroad workers covered under the Railroad Retirement Act use a separate but identically sized tier structure administered by the RRB; the OASDI-equivalent taxable maximum for 2026 is likewise $184,500, but payroll reporting runs through the RRB, not Form 941/W-2 Social Security boxes.
- Amounts above the base remain subject to Medicare HI tax (1.45% each) and to the Additional Medicare Tax where applicable; they are also not credited toward Social Security benefits.

verdict.summary:
# FMCSA Short-Haul (RODS) Exception — Radius and Release-Hour Limits

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Radius of the normal work reporting location within which the driver must operate | **150 air miles** (172.6 statute miles) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** |

Authority: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) — the '150 air-mile radius driver' short-haul exception. Jurisdiction: US federal (FMCSA), interstate/foreign commerce. The exemption relieves the driver of the records-of-duty-status requirement (49 CFR 395.8) and the supporting-documents requirement (49 CFR 395.11).

## 2. Governing text

49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) — a driver is exempt from 395.8 and 395.11 if all of the following hold:

- **(i) Radius.** 'The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location.'
- **(ii) Release.** 'The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours.'
- **(iii) Off-duty period.** (A) A property-carrying CMV driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty; (B) a passenger-carrying CMV driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty.
- **(iv) Time records.** The employing motor carrier maintains and retains for 6 months accurate and true time records showing: (A) the time the driver reports for duty each day; (B) total hours on duty each day; (C) the time the driver is released from duty each day; (D) the total time for the preceding 7 days per 395.8(j)(2) for drivers used for the first time or intermittently.

## 3. How each figure is measured (the part that decides pass/fail)

**Radius — air miles, not road miles.**
- 'Air miles' means straight-line (great-circle) distance between the normal work reporting location and the point in question. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles. These are the same threshold expressed in two units — do not treat 172.6 as a separate or additional limit.
- The boundary is measured from the *normal work reporting location* (the fixed location where the driver reports to and is released from work), not from the driver's residence, the terminal generally, or the day's first stop.
- The test is operational: every point the driver reaches during the tour must lie inside the 150 air-mile circle. Because the boundary is straight-line, a road route substantially longer than 150 miles can still qualify; conversely, a 140-road-mile trip around an obstruction can exceed 150 air miles. Verify with straight-line distance, and dispatch with a margin for GPS variance and rerouting rather than planning to the exact boundary.

**Release clock — 14 consecutive hours from coming on duty to release at the reporting location.**
- The clock starts when the driver reports for duty / comes on duty and stops only when the driver is *both* (a) back at the normal work reporting location *and* (b) released from work. Returning inside 14 hours but being held on duty past the 14th hour fails the condition.
- It is elapsed consecutive clock time. Off-duty time taken during the tour does not pause or extend it (same structural feature as the 395.3(a)(2) 14-hour window).
- Worked checks: report 06:00, released 19:45 → 13 h 45 m, qualifies. Report 06:00, released 20:15 → 14 h 15 m, does not qualify; the driver must keep RODS for that tour.
- The 14-hour release limit is not the 11-hour driving limit, not the 14-hour driving window of 395.3(a)(2), and not the 60/70-hour limit; those continue to apply on their own terms. The (e)(1) exemption is from 395.8 and 395.11 only.

**Driver-salesperson carve-out.** The return-and-release-within-14-hours condition in (e)(1)(ii) does not apply to a driver-salesperson (as defined in 395.2). All other (e)(1) conditions — radius, off-duty period, time records — still apply. For every other driver the 14-hour answer is unconditional.

**Property vs passenger.** Both classes use the same 150 air miles and the same 14 consecutive hours. The only difference in (e)(1) is the required off-duty period separating each 14 hours on duty: 10 consecutive hours for property-carrying, 8 consecutive hours for passenger-carrying. Neither difference changes the answers to asks 1 and 2.

## 4. Provisions that are often mistaken for this one (do not substitute their numbers)

| Provision | Radius | Hour figure | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| **395.1(e)(1)** — 150 air-mile radius driver | **150 air miles** | **released within 14 consecutive hours** | The short-haul RODS/ELD-supporting-document exception. This is the answer. |
| 395.1(e)(2) — property-carrying CMV not requiring a CDL | 150 air miles | return at end of each duty tour; no driving after the 14th hour on 5 days of any 7, and after the 16th hour on 2 days of any 7 | Separate exemption from 395.3(a)(2), 395.8, 395.11; drivers using it are ineligible for (e)(1), (g) and (o). The 16-hour allowance here is a two-days-per-week driving limit, not the release deadline for the general short-haul exception. |
| 395.1(o) — 16-hour exception | n/a | released within 16 hours after coming on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty; return to reporting location for the previous 5 duty tours; not used in the previous 6 consecutive days | A driving-window extension, not a RODS exemption. |
| 395.1(p) — motion picture production sites | **100 air miles** | separate daily driving limits follow | The only place the 100 air-mile figure appears in current Part 395 short-haul-adjacent text. It does not apply to general short-haul operations. |

Note on the '100 air-mile' label: some FMCSA ELD FAQ answers still use the phrase '100 air-mile radius (short-haul) exception'. That is legacy terminology from pre-2013 rule text; the current in-force short-haul radius in 395.1(e)(1) is 150 air miles. The same FAQ pages correctly state the operative test as 150 air miles with release within 14 hours, including for Canada/Mexico-domiciled drivers entering the US.

## 5. Compliance verification procedure

For each driver claimed under 395.1(e)(1), the carrier should be able to evidence all of the following on audit:

1. **Designated normal work reporting location** recorded for the driver (one fixed address per driver assignment).
2. **Radius test:** straight-line distance from that location to the farthest point served on the tour is ≤ 150 air miles. Keep the distance calculation or the geocoded route map with the driver's file.
3. **Release test:** daily time record shows report-for-duty time and release-from-duty time, with the interval ≤ 14 hours 00 minutes, and shows release occurring at the normal work reporting location.
4. **Off-duty test:** ≥ 10 consecutive hours off duty between tours for property-carrying drivers, ≥ 8 for passenger-carrying drivers.
5. **Records retention:** the above time records retained 6 months; for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, the preceding 7 days' total time per 395.8(j)(2) also retained.
6. **Failure handling:** any tour breaching 150 air miles or 14 consecutive hours is outside the exception — the driver must complete RODS (paper or ELD) for that tour. A pattern of breaches means the driver should not be managed as short-haul at all.

## 6. Caveats and verification notes

- The figures above are taken from the current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.1 and the 2024 printed CFR volume, both of which read 150 air miles and 14 consecutive hours. Confirm against the in-force 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) at the time of use, since notice-and-comment rulemaking can change either figure.
- State intrastate hours-of-service rules may set different radii or hour limits for drivers not in interstate commerce; this answer covers the federal FMCSA rule only.
- The exemption is conditional on all four (e)(1) elements. A driver who satisfies the radius and the 14-hour release but lacks the required off-duty period or the carrier's time records is not exempt.

IRC Section 402(g) limits the amount of retirement plan elective deferrals you may exclude from taxable income in your taxable year, which is generally the calendar year. Your 402(g) limit for 2024 is $23,000 (2023 is $22,500; 2022 is $20,500; $19,500 is 2020 and 2021).
The 402(g) limit applies to elective deferrals made by you to various plans, including:
401(k) plans,
403(b) arrangements,
Salary Reduction Simplified Employee Pension Plans (SAR-SEPs), and
Savings Incentive Match Plans for Employees (SIMPLE-IRAs).
The 402(g) limit is an individual limit and not a plan limit, so you must aggregate all elective deferrals contributed to all the plans in which you participate during the taxable year. For example, if you work for two different employers in 2022 that each have a 401(k) plan, you can only defer $20,500 in total - not $20,500 to each plan.

A 401(k) plan is a qualified plan that includes a feature allowing an employee to elect to have the employer contribute a portion of the employee’s wages to an individual account under the plan. The underlying plan can be a profit-sharing, stock bonus, pre-ERISA money purchase pension, or a rural cooperative plan. Generally, deferred wages (elective deferrals) are not subject to federal income tax withholding at the time of deferral, and they are not reported as taxable income on the employee’s individual income tax return.
401(k) plans are permitted to allow employees to designate some or all of their elective deferrals as “Roth elective deferrals” that are generally subject to taxation under the rules applicable to Roth IRAs. Roth deferrals are included in the employee's taxable income in the year of the deferral.

Automatic enrollment in a 401(k) plan
A 401(k) plan can have an automatic enrollment feature. This feature permits the employer to automatically reduce the employee’s wages by a fixed percentage or amount and contribute that amount to the 401(k) plan unless the employee has affirmatively chosen not to have his or her wages reduced or has chosen to have his or her wages reduced by a different percentage. These contributions qualify as elective deferrals. This has been an effective way for many employers to increase participation in their 401(k) plans. These contributions qualify as elective deferrals. For more information about 401(k) plans with an automatic enrollment feature, refer to Income Tax Regulations section 1.401(k)-1(A)(3)(ii).
Elective deferral limits
The law, under IRC section 402(g), limits the amount that a participant can defer on a pre-tax basis each year. See the 401(k) plan contribution limits.
Elective deferrals that exceed the section 402(g) dollar limit for a year or are recharacterized as after-tax contributions as part of a correction of the Actual Deferral Percentage (nondiscrimination) test are included in the employee’s gross income.

quotes.whole:
If the plan document permits, the employer can make matching contributions for an employee who contributes elective deferrals to the 401(k) plan. For example, a 401(k) plan might provide that the employer will contribute 50 cents for each dollar that participating employees choose to defer under the plan. As mentioned earlier, employer matching contributions may be subject to annual tests to determine if nondiscrimination requirements are met.
Other employer contributions
If the plan document permits, the employer can make additional contributions (other than matching contributions) for participants, including participants who choose not to contribute elective deferrals to the 401(k) plan. If the 401(k) plan is top-heavy, the employer may be required to make minimum contributions on behalf of certain employees. In general, a plan is top-heavy if the account balances of key employees exceed 60% of the account balances of all employees. The rules relating to the determination of whether a plan is top-heavy are complex. Please refer to section 1.416-1 of the Income Tax Regulations for the rules describing how to determine whether a plan is top-heavy.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

For tax year 2026, the limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals. It is an individual (not a plan) limit, and it is also capped at 100% of the employee's compensation — the operative rule is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of compensation. For any employee earning at least $24,500 in 2026, the binding number is $24,500.

AUTHORITY

- IRS Notice 2025-67, '2026 Amounts Relating to Retirement Plans and IRAs, as Adjusted for Changes in Cost-of-Living': 'The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.'
- IRS, 'COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions' (2026 cost-of-living adjustments, IR-2025-111), table '401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing plans, etc.': Elective deferrals — 2026: $24,500 (2025: $23,500; 2024: $23,000; 2023: $22,500).
- IRS, 'Retirement Topics — Contributions': 'The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.'

Both the statutory notice and the IRS limits table agree, so the figure is not a projection or an indexation estimate — it is the published 2026 amount.

WHAT THE $24,500 COVERS

- Applies to employee elective deferrals under a 401(k) plan: pre-tax salary reduction deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals alike. Roth and traditional deferrals share this one limit; designating deferrals as Roth does not create additional room.
- Automatic-enrollment contributions count as elective deferrals and consume the same $24,500.
- The limit is applied per individual per calendar year, not per plan. An employee who participates in more than one 401(k) plan (or a 401(k) plus a 403(b), SARSEP, or SIMPLE IRA) during 2026 must aggregate all elective deferrals across those plans against the single $24,500 figure. Deferring $24,500 into each of two plans is an excess deferral.
- Employer contributions — matching and nonelective — do not count against §402(g). They are tested against the separate §415(c) annual-additions limit ($72,000 for 2026).

WHAT IT EXCLUDES (context only — not part of the answer)

- Catch-up contributions under §414(v) are outside this figure. For 2026 the age-50-and-over catch-up limit is $8,000 (up from $7,500), and the SECURE 2.0 enhanced catch-up for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026 remains $11,250. A participant aged 50+ therefore has a total deferral capacity of $32,500 ($24,500 + $8,000) if the plan permits catch-ups.
- SIMPLE 401(k) plans are subject to a different deferral limit ($17,000 for 2026) and different catch-up amounts ($4,000 generally; $5,250 for ages 60–63). The $24,500 figure is for a traditional or safe harbor 401(k).
- Starter 401(k) deferral-only arrangements have their own limit ($6,000 for 2026, plus $1,100 for age 50+).
- The §415(c) annual-additions limit ($72,000 for 2026) and the annual compensation limit ($360,000 for 2026) are separate ceilings and do not change the $24,500 answer.

OPERATIONAL NOTES FOR THE PLAN

- $24,500 is the statutory maximum, not a floor. A plan document may impose a lower deferral cap (for example, a percentage-of-pay limit), and the plan's lower cap governs the participant. Confirm the plan's own deferral percentage/dollar cap before communicating a payroll figure.
- The limit is a calendar-year limit. Payroll must monitor year-to-date deferrals across the plan year, and for a participant who transferred from another employer's 401(k) during 2026, must obtain the prior plan's year-to-date deferral total to test the aggregated $24,500.
- Excess deferrals (amounts above $24,500, disregarding eligible catch-up) are includible in gross income for the year deferred and, if not corrected timely, are taxed again on distribution. Plans should have payroll controls verifying the §402(g) limit, with correction by distribution of excess deferrals plus allocable earnings.

SCOPE

US federal (IRS) rules only; assumes the employee is a standard participant in a traditional or safe harbor 401(k) and is asking for the base elective deferral limit excluding catch-up contributions. State law, non-US regimes, and plan-specific lower caps are outside this figure.
